result: Individual BBSome subunits were expressed in insect cells, but most showed poor solubility. Only BBS5, BBS9, and BBS18 were soluble in significant amounts when expressed individually, while other subunits co-purified with chaperones or were degraded.
evaluation: Claims C30-C33 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B. The SDS-PAGE gels clearly demonstrate expression of all subunits and differential solubility, with most subunits requiring co-expression for stability.

result: Co-expression studies identified stabilizing binary interactions between BBSome subunits. BBS9 emerged as a central organizational component forming stable interactions with BBS1, 2, 5, and 8. BBS18 with BBS4 and BBS9 with BBS8 showed the strongest solubility improvements. BBS chaperonins BBS6 and BBS12 stabilized each other but did not improve BBSome subunit yields.
evaluation: Claims C34-C37 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1 showing purified binary and multimeric complexes. The interaction network is consistent with prior immunoprecipitation studies (C35 cites Katoh et al., 2015), providing converging evidence for the proposed architecture.

result: BBS9 can be divided into an N-terminal β-propeller domain (residues 1-368) and a C-terminal domain (residues 363-887) with distinct binding specificities. The N-terminal domain binds BBS5 as a monomer, while the C-terminal domain binds BBS1 and forms dimers in gel filtration. Full-length BBS9 shows concentration-dependent dimerization.
evaluation: Claims C38-C43 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing gel filtration profiles and complex formation. The domain boundaries are consistent with prior structural predictions (Jin et al., 2010) and the dimerization behavior agrees with Knockenhauer and Schwartz, 2015.

result: A stable heterohexameric core BBSome complex composed of BBS1, 4, 5, 8, 9, and 18 was identified. BBS18 dramatically improved complex solubility and is crucial for linking BBS4 to the complex. The full 8-subunit BBSome with BBS2 and BBS7 was poorly soluble and oligomeric, while the 6-mer core was stable and monomeric. BBS chaperonins did not improve complex quality.
evaluation: Claims C44-C51 are supported by extensive biochemical data in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3. The gel filtration, SDS-PAGE, and purification data clearly demonstrate the superior stability of the 6-mer core over the full 8-mer complex. This is a key finding of the manuscript.

result: The 6-mer core BBSome could be purified in milligram quantities with high solubility (>150 µM or >50 mg/ml). The complex was resistant to high salt washes up to 2.5 M NaCl and eluted in gel filtration with an apparent molecular weight of ~400 kDa, consistent with the theoretical mass of 336.4 kDa for a monomer.
evaluation: Claims C52-C56 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C-E. The gel filtration profile, salt resistance, and purification yields demonstrate the exceptional stability of the core complex. The apparent MW is slightly higher than theoretical but within acceptable range for gel filtration, arguing against dimerization.

result: Negative stain electron microscopy revealed that the 6-mer core BBSome has a distorted Y-shape with pseudo 3-fold symmetry and a loosely packed architecture. The 3-D reconstruction achieved a resolution of ~23 Å.
evaluation: Claims C57-C59 are supported by EM data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The 2-D class averages and 3-D reconstruction clearly show the Y-shaped architecture. The resolution of 23 Å is appropriate for negative stain EM and was determined by standard FSC criteria.

result: The 6-mer core BBSome binds to Arl6•GppNHp in a nucleotide-dependent manner, with no detectable binding to Arl6•GDP, confirming the BBSome as an effector of Arl6.
evaluation: Claims C60-C61 are supported by pulldown data in Figure 3. The nucleotide-dependent binding is clearly demonstrated, with Arl6•GppNHp capturing most of the BBSome while Arl6•GDP shows no binding. This is consistent with the known role of Arl6 in BBSome recruitment.

result: The core BBSome binds to a truncated Smo receptor fragment (residues R546-L665) containing a ciliary targeting motif. The binding was detectable in pulldown assays but weaker than Arl6•GppNHp, with an affinity of 36.1 ± 3.9 µM measured by fluorescence polarization.
evaluation: Claims C62-C63 are supported by pulldown data in Figure 3 and fluorescence polarization measurements. The binding is clearly detectable but weaker than Arl6, consistent with the micromolar affinities typical of cargo-adapter interactions. The quantitative measurement provides important validation.

result: Peptide microarray screening identified BBSome binding sites in multiple cargo proteins. The core BBSome binds most strongly to peptides from the 3ICL and C-terminal regions of SSTR3 and other GPCRs, as well as to specific regions in Polycystin-1 containing a YEMV sorting signal. No binding was observed to VxPx or RVxP ciliary targeting signals.
evaluation: Claims C64-C68 are supported by peptide microarray data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The screening approach is unbiased and identifies binding regions consistent with prior literature on CTS sequences. The negative results for VxPx motifs are important controls showing specificity.

result: Fluorescence polarization measurements validated peptide microarray hits and determined dissociation constants. Multiple binding epitopes with variable affinities were identified. SSTR3 CT2 showed the highest affinity (0.11 ± 0.02 µM), while most tested peptides had KD values <25 µM. Smo peptides bound with affinities ranging from 1.1 to >100 µM depending on the region.
evaluation: Claims C69-C80 are supported by extensive fluorescence polarization data in Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and Table 1. The quantitative measurements validate the microarray results and reveal a range of affinities consistent with multiple binding modes. The data quality appears good with error estimates provided.

result: Mutational analysis of SSTR3 and Smo peptides showed that mutations of aromatic and basic residues significantly reduce BBSome binding affinity. For SSTR3, affinity is derived from three motifs (YR, FK, FRR) in an additive manner, with mutations reducing affinity 4-100 fold. For Smo, mutations of WRR or WCR motifs reduced affinity 9-13 fold.
evaluation: Claims C81-C86 are supported by mutational analysis data in Figure 5D-E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2. The systematic mutagenesis demonstrates that multiple aromatic/basic residues contribute to binding, with additive effects. This provides strong evidence for an extended binding site rather than a single consensus motif.

result: Arl6•GppNHp does not significantly affect the binding of cargo peptides (SSTR3 CT1, CT2, 3ICL) to the core BBSome in fluorescence polarization assays.
evaluation: Claim C87 is supported by experimental data in Figure 5A showing overlapping binding curves for BBSome alone versus BBSome + Arl6•GppNHp. This suggests Arl6 and cargo binding sites do not overlap or allosterically regulate each other, though the authors acknowledge this is based on peptide fragments.

result: The 6-mer core BBSome represents the complete set of BBSome subunits found in Drosophila, which lacks BBS2 and BBS7. These subunits appear dispensable for forming a stable monomeric complex that interacts with cargo and Arl6.
evaluation: Claims C88-C90 are supported by the experimental demonstration that the 6-mer core (lacking BBS2/7) binds both Arl6 and cargo, combined with knowledge that Drosophila lacks these subunits but has functional cilia. This provides evolutionary support for the functional sufficiency of the core complex.

result: The formation of a stable core BBSome without BBS chaperonins contrasts with prior studies suggesting BBS6, 10, and 12 are required for BBSome assembly. The authors propose that chaperonins may fold BBS2/7 before addition to the BBSome, a process that may not operate in insect cells, and that BBSome assembly might follow two parallel routes.
evaluation: Claims C91-C95 mix supported observations (C91-C92 based on experimental data) with speculative proposals (C93-C94). While the core BBSome formation without chaperonins is clearly demonstrated, the proposed dual assembly pathway is speculative and not directly tested. The insect cell system may not fully recapitulate mammalian assembly.

result: Based on domain-specific interactions and EM structure, the authors propose that the Y-shaped core BBSome has BBS1 and BBS5 in two lobes, with BBS4, 8, and 18 in the third lobe, held together by BBS9 as either a monomer or dimer.
evaluation: Claims C96-C98 are partially supported (C96 by experimental data on domain interactions) but largely speculative (C97-C98). The 23 Å resolution EM structure cannot localize individual subunits, so the proposed arrangement is inference from biochemical data. The oligomeric state of BBS9 in the complex remains unclear.

result: The core BBSome binds Arl6•GTP but not Arl6•GDP, with the interaction requiring only the BBS1 β-propeller. Cargo binding shows differential requirements: SSTR3 C-terminus requires the full core BBSome (110 nM affinity) with ~100-fold lower affinity to BBS1 alone, while SSTR3 3ICL binds similarly to BBS1 alone and the core BBSome, suggesting the C-terminus requires multiple subunits while 3ICL binding is primarily BBS1-mediated.
evaluation: Claims C99-C105 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5B and pulldown assays, combined with citations to prior work on Arl6-BBS1 interaction. The differential binding requirements for different SSTR3 regions provide important mechanistic insight into cargo recognition complexity.

result: Prior studies showed SSTR3 3ICL is sufficient to target non-ciliary GPCRs to cilia but removing it from SSTR3 does not prevent ciliary localization. For Smoothened, microarray data showed no significant BBSome binding to 3ICL but binding to C-terminal sequences. Prior studies found deletion of the 17-residue polybasic motif had minimal effect on BBS1 binding, while deletion of the 10-residue polybasic stretch enhanced binding. Neither polybasic motif strongly affects Smoothened ciliary localization.
evaluation: Claims C106-C111 accurately summarize prior literature (Berbari et al., 2008a; Zhang et al., 2012a; Nedelcu, 2013) and integrate it with the current microarray findings. This demonstrates that BBSome binding and ciliary localization are not simply correlated, an important conceptual point.

result: The BBSome contains an extended binding site recognizing general features of aromatic and basic residues rather than a specific sequence. Peptide walks showed enhanced binding when approaching arginine residues, with all tested GPCRs containing an arginine near the N-terminal start of the 3ICL. CTS sequences lacking aromatic/basic clustering (Ax(S/A)xQ, (I/V)KARK) were insufficient for core BBSome binding. Multiple aromatic/basic stretches are additive in enhancing affinity.
evaluation: Claims C112-C116 are supported by comprehensive peptide microarray data, mutational analysis, and sequence analysis. The conclusion of an extended binding site with additive contributions from multiple motifs is well-supported by the experimental evidence, though the claim remains somewhat speculative (C112) in proposing the general mechanism.

result: BBSome binding and ciliary targeting are not simply related. The BBSome is more important for export than import for certain proteins. The authors propose CTS might function as ciliary retention signals, with final protein localization determined by equilibrium of interactions inside and outside the cilium, which is dynamic and depends on signaling (e.g., Hedgehog pathway dramatically changes Smo and Ptch localization).
evaluation: Claims C117-C121 mix supported observations from prior literature (C118, C121 with citations) with speculative proposals (C119-C120). While the disconnect between BBSome binding and ciliary localization is well-documented, the proposed retention signal mechanism is speculative and not directly tested in this study.

result: The study identified a stable heterohexameric BBSome core complex that binds GPCRs with interactions only partially overlapping with previously described CTS, indicating more complex recognition than anticipated. Arl6•GTP does not affect BBSome-cargo interactions, suggesting no direct involvement in cargo loading/unloading. This stable complex enables future detailed biochemical and structural analysis.
evaluation: Claims C122-C126 accurately summarize the major findings of the manuscript. The core complex identification (C123), partial CTS overlap (C124), and lack of Arl6 effect on cargo binding (C125-C126) are all well-supported by the experimental data. C122 is a forward-looking statement about future work enabled by this study.
